claims.text: The coating consists of alternating nanoscale FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers.
The multilayer has significant compositional complexity, lattice distortion, and short-range order.
Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading is governed by enhanced interface-mediated processes.
Compositional complexity and lattice distortion impede conventional dislocation pile-up.
Compositional complexity and lattice distortion impede dislocation transmission.
Suppression of conventional dislocation processes promotes interface sliding.
Interface sliding is coupled with localized diffusion and dislocation climb.
Interface sliding, localized diffusion, and dislocation climb are the primary mechanisms of plastic flow.
Interfaces between the FCC and BCC layers locally modify dislocation behavior.
The interfaces act as localized barriers to conventional dislocation transmission.
Interface barriers lead to enhanced interface sliding, dislocation climb, and diffusion-assisted relaxation.
The proposed interface-mediated mechanism produces gradual progressive plasticity rather than sudden yielding.
Compared with conventional metallic multilayers, the high-entropy-alloy multilayer will accumulate plastic deformation more gradually under sustained load.
Deformed high-entropy-alloy multilayers will exhibit localized interface sliding.
Deformed high-entropy-alloy multilayers will exhibit diffusive dislocation motion across multilayer interfaces.
In conventional metallic multilayers such as Cu/Nb, dislocation pile-up and sudden interface-mediated shear events dominate plastic deformation.
The proposed mechanism requires a nanoscale multilayer architecture with maintained interface integrity.
Significant layer intermixing or severe temperature anomalies could invalidate the proposed mechanism.
Changing interface sharpness while holding layer thickness and creep conditions constant should change creep behavior if the interface-mediated hypothesis is correct.
